cli-basics.md:
## Why it exists

Before graphical windows, you talked to a computer by typing a line and reading the reply. That way of working never went away, because **text commands can be combined, repeated, saved and automated** in a way mouse clicks cannot. Every server you will ever deploy to, every container, every CI pipeline, every `git` command and most developer tools are driven from a **command line**. Learning it is the difference between "I clicked something and it worked once" and "here is the exact command, run it again".

Three words get mixed up, so pin them down:

- The **terminal** is the window that shows text and sends your keystrokes.
- The **shell** is the program inside it that reads your line, expands it and starts other programs. **bash** and **zsh** (the default on macOS) are shells; **PowerShell** is the Windows one. This lesson uses bash, and almost everything also works in zsh.
- A **command** is a program (`ls`, `grep`, `python3`) or a built-in of the shell (`cd`). You type `command option argument`, for example `ls -l notes`.

**Mental model:** the shell is a tiny language whose sentences are "run this program, with these arguments, wire its input and output to those places". You will use four ideas again and again: **where am I** (paths), **what is in here** (files), **connect these** (pipes) and **did it work** (exit status).

{{dg:0}}

## How it works

All transcripts below were produced by running the commands in a clean folder. Your paths will differ (here the demo folder is shown as `~/demo/cli`), and the first column `$` is the prompt, not something you type.

When you press Enter, the line travels down through these layers, and the reply comes back up as text:

{{dg:1}}

### Where am I: the working directory and paths

Every shell session is "in" one folder, the **working directory**. `pwd` prints it, `cd` changes it, `ls` lists it. A **path** says where a file is. An **absolute path** starts at the root `/` (`/home/ada/notes/todo.txt`). A **relative path** starts at the working directory (`notes/todo.txt`). Three shortcuts matter: `.` is "here", `..` is "the parent folder", `~` is your home folder.

```text
$ pwd
~/demo/cli
$ mkdir -p project/notes project/data
$ cd project
$ pwd
~/demo/cli/project
$ ls
data
notes
$ echo "buy milk" > notes/todo.txt
$ echo "call Sam" >> notes/todo.txt
$ cat notes/todo.txt
buy milk
call Sam
$ ls notes
todo.txt
$ cd ..
$ pwd
~/demo/cli
```

What happened, line by line:

- `mkdir -p a b` creates folders; `-p` also creates missing parents and does not complain if they exist.
- `>` **redirects** the output of `echo` into a file, replacing what was there; `>>` **appends**. Neither prints anything, which is normal: Unix commands are silent when they succeed.
- `cat file` prints a file. For long files use `less file` (quit with `q`) or `head -n 5 file` and `tail -n 5 file`.

Habits that save hours: press **Tab** to complete names, **Up** to recall the last command, **Ctrl+R** to search history, **Ctrl+C** to stop a running command, `cd -` to jump back to the previous folder, and `man ls` or `ls --help` to read the manual (on macOS, BSD tools differ slightly from the GNU ones used here).

### Copy, move, delete (and the missing undo)

```text
$ cp notes/todo.txt notes/todo.bak
$ mv notes/todo.bak data/todo-backup.txt
$ ls notes data
data:
access.log
todo-backup.txt
users.csv

notes:
todo.txt
$ rm data/todo-backup.txt
$ rm data/todo-backup.txt
rm: cannot remove 'data/todo-backup.txt': No such file or directory
$ ls -l notes/todo.txt | awk '{print $1, $5, $9}'
-rw-r--r-- 18 notes/todo.txt
```

`cp` copies, `mv` moves **or renames** (the same operation), `rm` deletes. There is **no recycle bin**: `rm` is permanent, and `rm -r folder` deletes a folder and everything under it. Read a destructive command twice, especially when it contains a variable or a `*`. `ls -l` shows permissions (`-rw-r--r--`: owner may read and write, everyone else may read), the size in bytes and the name.

### Pipes: small tools, joined together

Each program has three standard streams: **stdin** (input), **stdout** (normal output) and **stderr** (error messages). By default stdin is your keyboard and stdout and stderr are your screen. A **pipe** `|` connects the stdout of one command to the stdin of the next. That lets you build answers out of tiny, well-known tools. Here is a web server access log (time, method, path, status):

```text
09:00:01 GET /home 200
09:00:02 GET /login 200
09:00:05 POST /login 401
09:00:09 POST /login 200
09:01:13 GET /api/orders 200
09:01:14 GET /api/orders 500
09:02:30 GET /home 200
09:03:02 GET /missing 404
09:03:45 GET /api/orders 200
09:04:10 GET /home 200
```

Save it as `data/access.log` (for example by pasting it into an editor), then:

```text
$ wc -l data/access.log
10 data/access.log
$ head -n 3 data/access.log
09:00:01 GET /home 200
09:00:02 GET /login 200
09:00:05 POST /login 401
$ grep ' 500$' data/access.log
09:01:14 GET /api/orders 500
$ grep -c GET data/access.log
8
$ cut -d' ' -f3 data/access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn
      3 /login
      3 /home
      3 /api/orders
      1 /missing
$ awk '{print $4}' data/access.log | sort | uniq -c
      7 200
      1 401
      1 404
      1 500
$ grep -v ' 200$' data/access.log
09:00:05 POST /login 401
09:01:14 GET /api/orders 500
09:03:02 GET /missing 404
$ awk '$4 >= 400 {print $3, $4}' data/access.log
/login 401
/api/orders 500
/missing 404
$ tail -n 2 data/access.log
09:03:45 GET /api/orders 200
09:04:10 GET /home 200
```

The tools used here are worth memorising: `wc -l` counts lines, `grep` keeps lines that match (`-v` inverts, `-c` counts), `cut -d' ' -f3` takes the third space-separated field, `awk '{print $4}'` prints a column (and can compare numbers, as in `$4 >= 400`), `sort` orders, and `uniq -c` counts **adjacent** duplicates, which is why it is almost always preceded by `sort`. The pipeline `cut | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn` ("count how often each value appears, biggest first") is one of the most useful five-word sentences in computing.

### Streams, redirection and exit status

Errors travel on stderr, a separate stream, so they are not captured by `>`. Use `2>` to redirect them and `2>&1` to merge stderr into stdout. Every command also ends with an **exit status**, a number stored in `$?`. By convention **0 means success and anything else means failure**. `if`, `&&` (run the next command only if this one succeeded) and `||` (only if it failed) are built on it, and so is every CI system: a step "fails" when its command exits non-zero.

```text
$ ls /nope
ls: cannot access '/nope': No such file or directory
$ ls /nope 2> errors.txt
$ cat errors.txt
ls: cannot access '/nope': No such file or directory
$ ls /nope; echo "exit status: $?"
ls: cannot access '/nope': No such file or directory
exit status: 2
$ grep -q /home data/access.log; echo "exit status: $?"
exit status: 0
$ grep -q /zzz data/access.log; echo "exit status: $?"
exit status: 1
$ grep -q /home data/access.log && echo "found /home"
found /home
$ grep -q /zzz data/access.log || echo "no /zzz in the log"
no /zzz in the log
```

Note the exit statuses: `grep` returns 0 when it finds a match and 1 when it finds none (and 2 for a real error), so "not found" is a status, not an error message. That is why `grep -q` (quiet) is the standard way to ask a yes/no question.

### Variables, the environment and PATH

A shell variable is set with `NAME=value` (no spaces around `=`) and read with `$NAME`. A plain variable is private to the current shell. **`export NAME`** puts it into the **environment**, the set of variables copied to every program the shell starts. That is how settings such as `HOME`, `LANG` or `DATABASE_URL` reach your programs.

When you type a bare name such as `grep`, the shell searches the folders listed in the **`PATH`** environment variable, left to right, and runs the first match. `command -v name` tells you which file that would be and `type name` also tells you about built-ins and aliases.

```text
$ GREETING=hello
$ echo "$GREETING, world"
hello, world
$ bash -c 'echo "child sees: [$GREETING]"'
child sees: []
$ export GREETING
$ bash -c 'echo "child sees: [$GREETING]"'
child sees: [hello]
$ command -v grep
/usr/bin/grep
$ type cd
cd is a shell builtin
$ mkdir -p bin
$ printf '#!/usr/bin/env bash\necho "hello from my own command"\n' > bin/hello
$ chmod +x bin/hello
$ hello
bash: hello: command not found
$ PATH="$PWD/bin:$PATH" hello
hello from my own command
```

The unexported variable was invisible to the child process; after `export` it was visible. And `hello` was "command not found" until its folder was put at the front of `PATH` for one command. This is also why **a program in the current folder is not found by name**: you must write `./backup.sh` (a path) unless `.` is on `PATH`, which it should not be.

### Quoting and globbing: what the shell does before your program runs

Before starting a program, the shell **expands** your line. It replaces variables, and it replaces patterns such as `*.txt` with the matching file names (**globbing**). Then it splits the result into words on spaces. The program never sees the `*`; it just receives the list of names.

```text
$ mkdir -p files
$ cd files
$ touch "my report.txt" a.txt b.txt c.md
$ ls *.txt
a.txt
b.txt
my report.txt
$ ls "my report.txt"
my report.txt
$ ls my report.txt
ls: cannot access 'my': No such file or directory
ls: cannot access 'report.txt': No such file or directory
$ echo *.md
c.md
$ echo "*.md"
*.md
```

The file `my report.txt` has a space. Quoted, it is one argument. Unquoted, `ls my report.txt` became two arguments, `my` and `report.txt`, and both failed. The same splitting happens to variables, so the rule is: **always quote variable expansions, `"$var"`**, unless you specifically want splitting. Single quotes `'...'` turn all expansion off; double quotes allow `$var`.

## Worked example

Goal: a reusable `backup.sh` that copies a folder to `backup-<name>` and reports what it did, failing loudly when used wrongly.

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

src="${1:?usage: backup.sh SOURCE_DIR}"
dest="backup-$(basename "$src")"

mkdir -p "$dest"
cp -r "$src"/. "$dest"/
echo "copied $(find "$dest" -type f | wc -l) files to $dest"
```

Line by line:

- `#!/usr/bin/env bash` is the **shebang**: the first two characters tell the operating system which interpreter should run the file when you execute it directly.
- `set -euo pipefail` makes the script stop at the first failing command (`-e`), treat unset variables as errors (`-u`) and fail a pipeline if any stage fails (`pipefail`). Without it a shell script happily continues after errors.
- `"${1:?usage: ...}"` reads the first argument and aborts with a message if it is missing.
- `"$dest"` and `"$src"` are quoted, so names with spaces work. `$(...)` runs a command and substitutes its output.

```text
$ ./backup.sh data
bash: ./backup.sh: Permission denied
$ chmod +x backup.sh
$ ./backup.sh data
copied 2 files to backup-data
$ ./backup.sh; echo "exit status: $?"
./backup.sh: line 4: 1: usage: backup.sh SOURCE_DIR
exit status: 1
$ ls
backup-data
backup.sh
bin
data
errors.txt
files
notes
```

Three lessons are visible: a new file is **not executable** until `chmod +x` (permission denied); running it with an argument works; running it without one prints the usage message and exits with status 1, which a calling script or CI job can detect. Finally two commands you will use constantly:

```text
$ find . -name "*.txt" | sort
./errors.txt
./files/a.txt
./files/b.txt
./files/my report.txt
./notes/todo.txt
$ ln -s data/access.log latest.log
$ ls -l latest.log | awk '{print $1, $9, $10, $11}'
lrwxrwxrwx latest.log -> data/access.log
$ tail -n 1 latest.log
09:04:10 GET /home 200
```

`find . -name "*.txt"` searches a whole tree (the shell did not expand the pattern because it was quoted, so `find` itself received `*.txt`), and `ln -s target link` creates a **symbolic link**, a small file that points at another path (`->` in `ls -l`).

## In real products

- **Servers and containers.** You reach a production machine over `ssh` and have only a shell. Debugging "why is the disk full" or "why is this process using memory" is `df -h`, `du -sh *`, `ps`, `grep` on log files and `tail -f` to follow a log live.
- **CI/CD.** A GitHub Actions or GitLab job is a list of shell commands. The job fails because a command returned a non-zero exit status; understanding `$?`, `&&` and `set -e` explains most red pipelines.
- **Dockerfiles and Makefiles** are mostly shell commands with a thin layer on top; the `RUN` lines in a Dockerfile are executed by `/bin/sh`.
- **Everyday developer tools** (`git`, `npm`, `pip`, `docker`, `kubectl`, `terraform`, `aws`) are all commands with sub-commands, flags and exit statuses. The same skills apply to each.
- **When a script outgrows bash.** Once you need data structures, real error handling or more than about fifty lines, switch to Python or Node. Shell is glue; it is a poor place for logic.

> [!pitfall] `rm -rf` with an empty or wrong variable (`rm -rf "$DIR/"` when `DIR` is unset expands to `rm -rf /`). Use `set -u`, quote variables, print the command with `echo` first, and prefer `rm -ri` or moving to a trash folder when unsure. Shell has no undo.

> [!pitfall] Forgetting quotes around variables and paths. Names with spaces split into several arguments, and a value that starts with `-` can be read as an option. Write `"$file"`, and `--` to end options (`rm -- "$file"`).

> [!pitfall] Using `>` when you meant `>>`. `echo x > log.txt` **overwrites** the file. `sort file > file` empties the file before `sort` reads it; write to a new file and move it into place.

> [!pitfall] Assuming every machine has the same tools. macOS ships BSD versions of `sed`, `date`, `ls` and others whose flags differ from the GNU versions on Linux, and many minimal containers have only `sh`, not `bash`. Check with `command -v` and read `man` on the target system.

> [!tip] Learn to read before you write: run `command --help`, `man command`, or paste a command into explainshell.com. Build pipelines one stage at a time, running each prefix to check its output before adding `| next`. Run `shellcheck script.sh` on every script you keep.

> [!tip] Put reusable scripts in a folder on your `PATH` (commonly `~/.local/bin` or `~/bin`), and keep short, dated notes of commands that solved a problem; most of your future self's commands are your past self's commands.

> [!cost] Shell time is mostly human time: a long one-liner nobody can read is expensive to debug. A script that runs `find / -name x` on a large disk, or `grep -r` over a huge folder, can also hammer disk and CPU on a shared server. Scope searches to a folder and run heavy jobs off-peak or with `nice`.

> [!security] Treat anything copied from a web page as untrusted: a pasted command can hide extra lines or invisible characters. Never run `curl ... | sudo bash` from a source you have not read, never put passwords or API keys directly in a command (they end up in your shell history and in `ps` output; read them from an environment variable or a prompt), and use `sudo` only for the one command that needs it. Keep file permissions tight: a private key must not be readable by others (`chmod 600`).

> [!prod] Production checklist for a script: starts with a shebang and `set -euo pipefail`; quotes every expansion; validates its arguments; prints what it is about to do; exits non-zero on failure; logs to stderr for errors; passes `shellcheck`; and is stored in version control, not in someone's home folder.

> [!version] Verified 2026-10-22 in the sandbox on Linux with GNU bash 5.2.21 and GNU coreutils/findutils/grep/awk: every transcript above was produced by running the commands in a fresh folder (the folder path was replaced by `~/demo`, and a "line N:" prefix in some shell error messages was shortened to `bash:`). The script `backup.sh`, the exit statuses, globbing, quoting and PATH demonstrations were all observed. NOT verified: zsh, macOS/BSD tool flags and PowerShell behaviour (described from general knowledge), the Windows Subsystem for Linux, and the linked resources, which could not be opened from the offline sandbox.
q: A command prints an error and you want to save only the error text to a file. Which redirection do you use, and why does `>` not work?
Use `command 2> errors.txt`. Error messages are written to stderr (stream 2), while `>` redirects only stdout (stream 1), so the error would still appear on screen.
`grep -q /zzz access.log; echo $?` prints 1. Did the command fail?

Not in the sense of a crash: grep uses status 0 for 'found', 1 for 'no match' and 2 for a real error. Scripts and CI treat any non-zero status as failure, so use `||` or `if` deliberately when 'no match' is acceptable.
You run `./deploy.sh` and get 'Permission denied', but the file exists. What are the two likeliest causes and fixes?

The file is not executable (fix: `chmod +x deploy.sh`), or you lack permission for the file or a folder on its path (check `ls -l` and the owner). Also remember that a script in the current folder must be run as `./deploy.sh`, not `deploy.sh`.

linux-shell.md:
## Why it exists

Almost every server you will ever deploy to runs Linux: your containers, your cloud VMs, your CI runners, the machines behind managed services. When something breaks at 3 a.m. there is often no graphical tool, only a terminal over SSH. The **shell** is the interface to that world, and its power comes from one idea: small programs that each do one thing, connected by text streams, can be combined into tools nobody had to write in advance. Learning it once pays off for decades, because the core commands have barely changed since the 1980s.

**Mental model:** in Unix everything is either a **file** or a **process**. Files include regular files, directories, devices (`/dev`), and even live kernel information (`/proc`). Processes are running programs with an owner, an environment, open files and three standard streams: **stdin** (input), **stdout** (output) and **stderr** (errors). The shell starts processes and wires their streams together with pipes and redirects. If you can answer "which process, which file, which user, which permission?", you can debug most Linux problems.

{{dg:0}}

## How it works

### The filesystem layout

Linux has one tree starting at `/`. The directories worth knowing: `/etc` (system configuration, plain text), `/var/log` (logs), `/var/lib` (service data such as databases), `/home` (user files), `/tmp` (temporary files, often wiped on reboot), `/usr/bin` and `/usr/local/bin` (programs), `/opt` (add-on software), `/proc` and `/sys` (live views into the kernel, not real disk files) and `/dev` (devices). Paths are case-sensitive, hidden files start with a dot, and `~` means your home directory. A path starting with `/` is absolute; otherwise it is relative to the current directory (`pwd`).

### Moving around and looking at things

`ls -la` (long listing with hidden files), `cd`, `pwd`, `cat`, `less` (scroll a file; `q` quits, `/text` searches), `head -n 20`, `tail -n 100`, and **`tail -f file`** (follow a log live). `file` tells you what a file is, `stat` shows metadata, `du -sh *` shows sizes, and `df -h` shows free space per filesystem. `man command` and `command --help` are always available offline.

### Searching and the text toolbox

- **`grep`** finds lines matching a pattern: `grep -rn "timeout" /etc/myapp`, `-i` ignore case, `-v` invert, `-C 3` show context. **`rg` (ripgrep)** is a faster modern alternative.
- **`find`** locates files by name, type, size or age: `find /var/log -name "*.log" -mtime +7`. **`fd`** is a friendlier alternative.
- **`sort`, `uniq -c`, `cut`, `tr`, `wc -l`, `head`/`tail`** are the building blocks for counting and slicing.
- **`awk`** processes columns (`awk '{print $1, $9}'`), **`sed`** edits streams (`sed 's/old/new/g'`), **`jq`** queries JSON, **`xargs`** turns lines into command arguments.

### Pipes, redirects and exit codes

`cmd1 | cmd2` sends cmd1's stdout into cmd2's stdin. `>` writes stdout to a file (overwriting), `>>` appends, `2>` redirects stderr, and `2>&1` merges stderr into stdout, so `cmd > out.log 2>&1` captures everything. `tee` writes to a file and still passes data along. Every command returns an **exit code**: `0` means success, anything else is failure, and `$?` holds the last one. That is how `&&` ("run the next only if this succeeded") and `||` work, and how CI knows a step failed.

**Quoting matters.** Unquoted variables are split on spaces and expanded as globs, so `rm $file` with a space in the name deletes the wrong things. Quote them: `rm -- "$file"`. Single quotes are literal; double quotes still expand `$variables`.

### Users, groups and permissions

Every file has an owner, a group and permission bits for **user, group, other**, each with **r**ead, **w**rite, e**x**ecute. `ls -l` shows `-rwxr-xr--`: the owner can read, write and execute; the group can read and execute; everyone else can only read. `chmod 640 file` sets bits numerically (r=4, w=2, x=1), `chmod +x script.sh` makes it runnable, and `chown user:group file` changes ownership. For directories, execute means "may enter". `umask` sets the default permissions for new files. **`sudo`** runs a single command as root; prefer it to logging in as root, and grant it narrowly. Setuid and setgid bits (`s`) make a program run with its owner's privileges and are a classic security risk when misapplied.

### Processes and signals

`ps aux`, `top` or `htop` show what is running; `pgrep -a name` finds processes by name. A **signal** is a message to a process: `SIGTERM` (15, the default of `kill PID`) asks it to shut down gracefully, `SIGINT` is Ctrl+C, `SIGHUP` often means "reload config", and `SIGKILL` (9) kills immediately with no cleanup and cannot be caught. Always try SIGTERM first and give it seconds to flush buffers and close connections; reach for `kill -9` only when it ignores you. `command &` runs in the background, `jobs`, `fg`, `bg` manage them, `nohup` keeps a process alive after you disconnect (but a service manager is better).

### Services with systemd

Most modern distributions use **systemd** to start and supervise services. `systemctl status nginx`, `systemctl restart nginx`, `systemctl enable --now nginx` (start and enable at boot), and **`journalctl -u nginx -f`** (follow that service's logs, `-n 200` for recent lines, `--since "1 hour ago"`). A **unit file** describes a service: the command, the user, restart policy and dependencies, as in the worked example. systemd timers are the modern alternative to cron for scheduled jobs.

### Networking tools

`ip addr` (interfaces and IPs), `ss -tulpn` (which process listens on which port), `curl -v https://host/path` (see the full HTTP exchange, headers and TLS), `dig example.com` (DNS), `ping`, `traceroute`, `nc -vz host 5432` (is a TCP port reachable?), and `lsof -i :3000` (who has port 3000?). "Connection refused" means nothing is listening on that port; a timeout usually means a firewall or routing problem; "no route to host" or a DNS failure means you never reached the machine.

### SSH, keys and copying files

`ssh user@host` opens a remote shell. Use **key pairs** (`ssh-keygen -t ed25519`): the private key stays on your machine with permissions `600` (SSH refuses to use a key others can read), and the public key goes into `~/.ssh/authorized_keys` on the server. `~/.ssh/config` lets you name hosts and set users and keys. **Port forwarding** (`ssh -L 5432:localhost:5432 bastion`) reaches a private database through a jump host. Copy with `scp` or, better for repeated syncs, `rsync -avz --progress src/ user@host:/dest/`. Add `-n` (dry run) to rsync before you trust a command with `--delete`.

### Packages and the environment

`apt` (Debian and Ubuntu), `dnf` (Fedora, RHEL and relatives), `apk` (Alpine, common in containers) and Homebrew on macOS install software. Environment variables (`export NAME=value`, `printenv`) configure programs; **`PATH`** is the ordered list of directories searched for commands. `which cmd` and `type cmd` show which one will run. On macOS the userland is BSD-flavored, so some flags differ from GNU/Linux (for example `sed -i ''`); on Windows use WSL 2 for a real Linux environment.

### Shell scripts that do not bite you

Start scripts with `#!/usr/bin/env bash` and `set -euo pipefail` (exit on error, on undefined variables, and fail a pipeline if any stage fails). Quote variables, use functions, check inputs, clean up with `trap`, and run **ShellCheck**, a linter that catches most quoting and logic mistakes. When a script grows past a hundred or so lines or needs data structures, switch to Python.

### A debugging method that works

{{dg:1}}

For "the server is slow or down": check **resources** first (`uptime` for load, `free -h` for memory, `df -h` and `df -i` for disk and inodes, `top` for CPU hogs), then the **process** (is it running, what port is it listening on, is it being restarted?), then the **logs** (`journalctl`, `/var/log`, app logs), form one hypothesis, change one thing, verify, and write down what you found. Most outages are one of: disk full, out of memory (the kernel killed a process), a crashed or misconfigured service, a full connection limit, an expired certificate, or DNS.

## Worked example

**1) Answer a real question with a pipeline:** "which URLs returned the most 500 errors today?" from an nginx-style access log whose 9th field is the status and 7th is the path:

```bash
grep -h " 500 " /var/log/nginx/access.log \
  | awk '{print $7}' \
  | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -5
```

Each stage is one small tool: filter, extract a column, count duplicates, sort by count, keep the top five. Replace `grep` with `zgrep` for rotated `.gz` logs.

**2) A robust backup script**, with strict mode, argument checks, cleanup and a verifiable result:

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

usage() { echo "usage: $0 SOURCE_DIR DEST_DIR [KEEP_DAYS]" >&2; exit 2; }
[[ $# -ge 2 ]] || usage
src=$1; dest=$2; keep=${3:-7}
[[ -d "$src" ]] || { echo "source not found: $src" >&2; exit 1; }
mkdir -p -- "$dest"

stamp=$(date -u +%Y%m%dT%H%M%SZ)
tmp=$(mktemp -d)
trap 'rm -rf -- "$tmp"' EXIT                    # always clean up, even on error

archive="$tmp/backup-$stamp.tar.gz"
tar -czf "$archive" -C "$src" .
tar -tzf "$archive" > /dev/null                 # verify the archive is readable
mv -- "$archive" "$dest/"
echo "wrote $dest/backup-$stamp.tar.gz"

# prune old backups, carefully: only our own files, only older than KEEP_DAYS
find "$dest" -maxdepth 1 -name 'backup-*.tar.gz' -mtime +"$keep" -print -delete
```

**3) Run it as a service on a schedule with systemd**, instead of leaving a script in someone's crontab. A one-shot service plus a timer:

```ini
# /etc/systemd/system/backup.service
[Unit]
Description=Nightly backup

[Service]
Type=oneshot
User=backup
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/backup.sh /srv/app/data /var/backups/app 14
```

```ini
# /etc/systemd/system/backup.timer
[Unit]
Description=Run backup nightly

[Timer]
OnCalendar=*-*-* 02:30:00
Persistent=true

[Install]
WantedBy=timers.target
```

```bash
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl enable --now backup.timer
systemctl list-timers backup.timer      # confirm the next run
journalctl -u backup.service -n 50      # see the output of the last run
```

**4) A long-running app as a supervised service:**

```ini
# /etc/systemd/system/myapp.service
[Unit]
Description=My app
After=network-online.target
Wants=network-online.target

[Service]
User=myapp
WorkingDirectory=/srv/myapp
EnvironmentFile=/etc/myapp/env            # secrets here, mode 600, owned by root
ExecStart=/srv/myapp/.venv/bin/gunicorn app:app -b 127.0.0.1:8000
Restart=on-failure
RestartSec=3
NoNewPrivileges=true
ProtectSystem=strict
ReadWritePaths=/var/lib/myapp

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
```

Try it on a throwaway VM or container: start the service, `kill -9` its main process and watch systemd restart it (`journalctl -u myapp -f`); then break the `ExecStart` path and read the failure reason in `systemctl status`.

## In real products

- **Cloud servers and containers:** EC2, Azure VMs, GKE and EKS nodes and nearly every Docker image run Linux, usually Debian, Ubuntu, Alpine, Amazon Linux or a Red Hat relative. Containers are ordinary Linux processes isolated with namespaces and cgroups (see the OS lesson).
- **CI systems** such as GitHub Actions run your build as shell steps on Linux runners, and a step "fails" exactly when a command exits non-zero, which is why `set -e` and exit codes matter.
- **Incident response** at every company starts with the same commands: `top`, `df`, `ss`, `journalctl`, `tcpdump`, and a look at recent deploys. Teams write them into runbooks so that anyone on call can follow them.
- **Infrastructure tools** (Ansible, Terraform provisioners, cloud-init, Kubernetes init containers) mostly drive shell commands over SSH or at boot. Understanding the shell means understanding what they actually do.
- **Observability agents and log shippers** read files under `/var/log` and `/proc`; the OpenTelemetry and cloud monitoring agents are system services managed by systemd.

> [!pitfall] Running `rm -rf` with an unquoted or empty variable (`rm -rf $DIR/`). If `DIR` is empty this becomes `rm -rf /`. Quote variables, use `set -u` so unset variables abort the script, and test destructive commands with `echo` or a dry run first.
> [!pitfall] Using `kill -9` as a first resort. The process cannot flush buffers, release locks or finish writes, which corrupts files and leaves stale lock and PID files. Send SIGTERM, wait, then escalate.
> [!pitfall] Fixing permission errors with `chmod 777`. It makes the file writable by every user and process on the machine, hides the real cause (wrong owner or group), and is a common route to privilege escalation. Find the owning user and grant exactly what is needed.
> [!pitfall] Parsing `ls` output or assuming filenames are simple. Names can contain spaces, newlines and leading dashes. Use globs, `find -print0 | xargs -0`, and `--` before filename arguments.
> [!pitfall] "Disk full" with space apparently free: you can also run out of **inodes** (`df -i`), or a deleted file may still be held open by a process (`lsof +L1`). Check both before deleting more data.
> [!security] Harden SSH: key-based login only (`PasswordAuthentication no`), no direct root login (`PermitRootLogin no`), a firewall that exposes only needed ports, and automatic security updates. Protect private keys (mode 600, passphrase, ssh-agent), never paste secrets into commands that land in shell history, and be skeptical of `curl ... | sudo bash` from sources you have not read.
> [!prod] Do not hand-edit production servers. Put configuration in version control, deploy with automation (images, Terraform, Ansible), run services under systemd with a dedicated unprivileged user and a restart policy, and ship logs off the box. A server you cannot rebuild from code is a liability.
> [!cost] Idle and oversized machines are the cheapest bill to cut. Learn `top`, `free` and `iostat` well enough to see whether a VM is memory-bound, CPU-bound or just idle, and right-size it. Rotate and compress logs (logrotate or journald limits) so they do not fill disks or drive up storage and shipping costs.
> [!tip] Keep a personal file of one-liners you reuse (the log pipeline, the port check, the disk-usage ranking) and turn the good ones into functions or scripts. Fluency with five or six tools (`grep`, `find`, `awk`, `sort`, `xargs`, `jq`) covers most real tasks.
q: What is the difference between SIGTERM and SIGKILL, and which should you send first?
SIGTERM asks a process to shut down and can be caught, letting it flush data and close connections. SIGKILL cannot be caught and gives no chance to clean up. Send SIGTERM first, wait, then escalate.
What does `cmd > out.log 2>&1` do?
It redirects stdout to out.log and then redirects stderr (file descriptor 2) to wherever stdout now points, so both streams are captured in the file.
What does the permission string -rw-r----- mean, and what chmod value is it?
The owner can read and write, the group can read, and others have no access. In numeric form that is 640.
Why add `set -euo pipefail` to bash scripts?
-e exits on a failing command, -u treats unset variables as errors, and pipefail makes a pipeline fail if any stage fails. Together they stop scripts from silently continuing after errors.
A disk looks only half full but writes fail with no space left. What else do you check?
Inode exhaustion with df -i, and deleted files still held open by processes with lsof +L1. Either can fill a filesystem without using visible space.
What does `Connection refused` versus a timeout tell you when connecting to a port?
Refused means the host answered and nothing is listening on that port (or it actively rejected). A timeout usually means packets are dropped by a firewall, security group or routing problem.

os-concepts.md:
## Why it exists

Your code never talks to hardware. It runs inside a **process** that the operating system created, gets CPU time when the **scheduler** allows it, sees memory the OS has arranged to look private and contiguous, and reads files and network sockets only by asking the kernel. Almost every mysterious production behavior has an operating-system explanation: why a container was killed with exit code 137, why one slow disk made a whole service stall, why adding threads did not speed up a Python program, why Node can serve thousands of connections on one thread, why a database insists on `fsync`. Knowing the model turns these from folklore into things you can reason about and measure.

**Mental model:** the OS is a **resource manager and illusionist**. It gives each program the illusion of owning a CPU (by switching between them thousands of times a second), owning all of memory (virtual memory), and owning clean, uniform files and sockets (file descriptors), while enforcing isolation so one program cannot read or corrupt another. The price of each illusion is overhead: context switches, page faults, system calls. Performance work is mostly about avoiding those costs or hiding them with concurrency.

{{dg:0}}

## How it works

### User mode, kernel mode and system calls

The CPU runs your code in **user mode**, which cannot touch hardware directly. To do anything privileged (read a file, send a packet, allocate memory, start a process) your program makes a **system call** (`read`, `write`, `open`, `mmap`, `fork`, `epoll_wait`), a controlled jump into the **kernel**, which does the work and returns. A syscall costs roughly hundreds of nanoseconds to a few microseconds, so programs batch work (buffered I/O, writing 64 KB once rather than a byte 65,536 times). `strace -c -p PID` counts a process's syscalls; it often shows at a glance whether a program is stuck waiting on I/O.

### Processes and threads

A **process** is a running program with its own virtual address space, open files, environment and PID. `fork()` creates a child that starts as a copy (with **copy-on-write**: memory pages are shared until one side modifies them, so forking is cheap), and `exec()` replaces its program. Shells, servers and container runtimes are built from fork and exec. When a child exits, its parent must collect its exit status (`wait`), or it lingers as a **zombie** entry; if the parent dies first, the child is adopted by PID 1. This is why the first process in a container must handle signals and reap children properly.

A **thread** is an independent flow of execution **inside** a process. Threads share the process's memory (cheap to communicate, dangerous to coordinate) but have their own stack and registers. Processes are isolated and heavier; threads are lighter but share fate: one bad write corrupts every thread, and one crash kills the whole process. Languages add their own layers on top: Python's **GIL** lets only one thread run Python bytecode at a time (so threads help I/O-bound work but not CPU-bound work, where you use processes or native extensions), Go schedules goroutines onto a few OS threads, and Node runs JavaScript on one thread with a pool for blocking work.

### Scheduling and context switches

There are usually more runnable threads than CPU cores, so the **scheduler** gives each a **time slice** (a few milliseconds) and **preempts** it with a timer interrupt, choosing the next by priority and fairness (Linux's default is the Completely Fair Scheduler lineage, with `nice` values and real-time classes available). Moving the CPU from one thread to another is a **context switch**: save registers, swap memory mappings, and likely lose warm CPU caches. A direct switch costs on the order of a few microseconds, and the indirect cache-miss cost is often bigger. Consequences: thousands of busy threads can spend more time switching than working; a CPU-bound task and a latency-sensitive task on the same core hurt each other; and "load average" counts both running and waiting-for-disk tasks, so a high load with low CPU use means I/O waits.

### Synchronization, races and deadlocks

When threads share data, interleavings matter. A **race condition** is a bug whose outcome depends on timing: two threads do `counter += 1` (read, add, write) and updates are lost. The fixes are **mutual exclusion** (a **mutex** or lock protecting a **critical section**), **atomic operations**, **semaphores** (a counter allowing N holders, used for pools and rate limits), **condition variables** (wait until something is true), message passing, or immutable data. Locks bring **deadlock**: two threads each hold one lock and wait for the other's. A deadlock needs all four conditions (mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, circular wait), so you prevent it by breaking one: acquire locks in a single global order, use timeouts, or hold fewer locks.

### Virtual memory

Each process addresses **virtual memory**, which the hardware (the MMU, with the TLB as a translation cache) maps to physical RAM in fixed-size **pages** (commonly 4 KB). This gives isolation (a process cannot name another's memory), flexibility (memory need not be contiguous physically) and tricks: lazy allocation, memory-mapped files (`mmap`), shared libraries mapped once and shared, and copy-on-write.

- A **page fault** occurs when a page is not mapped yet. A *minor* fault (allocate or map a page already in memory) costs around a microsecond; a *major* fault (read from disk or swap) costs milliseconds, thousands of times more.
- **The page cache:** the kernel caches file data in otherwise-unused RAM, so repeated reads are memory-speed and "free memory" looks low on a healthy Linux machine. Check `available` in `free -h`, not `free`.
- **Swap** moves cold pages to disk to free RAM. A little is harmless; constant swapping (thrashing) makes everything crawl.
- **The OOM killer:** when memory is truly exhausted the kernel kills a process to survive. In containers, a **cgroup memory limit** triggers the same thing at the container boundary; the process dies with SIGKILL, shown as exit code **137** (128 + 9). The fix is almost never "retry"; it is a memory leak, an unbounded cache, a too-small limit or too many workers.
- **Stack versus heap:** each thread has a fixed-size stack (local variables, call frames; overflow means deep recursion), while the heap holds dynamic allocations managed by the runtime or garbage collector. **RSS** is the physical memory a process actually uses; **VSZ** is the virtual size, which is usually much larger and not alarming by itself.

### Files, descriptors and durability

A **file descriptor** (fd) is a small integer the kernel gives your process to refer to an open file, pipe, socket or device; `0`, `1`, `2` are stdin, stdout, stderr. Each process has a limit (`ulimit -n`), and a server that leaks descriptors eventually fails with "too many open files". A write to a file normally lands in the **page cache** and returns immediately; the kernel flushes to disk later. **`fsync`** forces data to stable storage, which is why databases call it on commit and why durability settings (Postgres `fsync`, Redis `appendfsync`, Kafka flush policy) trade speed for safety: without it, a power loss can lose acknowledged writes. Filesystems use **journaling** to stay consistent after crashes.

### Blocking, non-blocking I/O and the event loop

A **blocking** `read()` on a socket puts the thread to sleep until data arrives. One thread per connection works for hundreds of clients but costs memory (a stack each) and context switches at tens of thousands. The alternative is **non-blocking** I/O with a readiness API: you give the kernel a set of descriptors and ask "which are ready?" with **`epoll`** (Linux), **`kqueue`** (BSD and macOS) or **IOCP** (Windows); older `select` and `poll` scan the whole set each time, which does not scale. A single thread loops: wait for readiness, handle whatever is ready, repeat. That is the **event loop** inside Node.js (libuv), Python's `asyncio`, Nginx and Redis, and it is why one thread can juggle tens of thousands of mostly idle connections. The catch: any CPU-heavy or blocking call inside the loop stalls every connection. **`io_uring`** is a newer Linux interface that submits batches of I/O requests through shared rings to avoid per-call syscall overhead.

{{dg:1}}

### Inter-process communication

Processes talk through **pipes** (`a | b`), **Unix domain sockets** (fast local sockets, used by Docker and databases), **TCP sockets** (across machines), **shared memory** (fastest, needs your own synchronization), **signals** (tiny notifications such as SIGTERM) and files. Choose by isolation, speed and whether the peers may be on different machines.

### Containers are processes with walls

A container is not a small VM. It is an ordinary Linux process (or group) started with **namespaces** (separate views of process IDs, network, mounts, hostnames, users) and limited by **cgroups** (caps on CPU, memory and I/O). It shares the host kernel, which is why containers start in milliseconds, why a kernel vulnerability affects all of them, and why `docker stats` numbers and a container's OOM kills come from cgroups. Virtual machines add a hypervisor and a separate kernel per guest for stronger isolation at higher cost.

## Worked example

Four small experiments you can run on any Linux machine or macOS (a few details differ), using only the Python standard library.

**1) Threads and the GIL, CPU-bound versus I/O-bound.** Compare sequential, threaded and multi-process runs:

```python
import time, threading, multiprocessing as mp

def burn(n=3_000_000):                    # CPU-bound: pure Python loop
    s = 0
    for i in range(n):
        s += i * i
    return s

def wait_io(seconds=0.5):                 # I/O-bound: sleeping stands in for a network call
    time.sleep(seconds)

def timeit(label, fn):
    t = time.perf_counter(); fn(); print(f"{label:28s} {time.perf_counter() - t:5.2f}s")

def run_threads(fn, k=4):
    ts = [threading.Thread(target=fn) for _ in range(k)]
    [t.start() for t in ts]; [t.join() for t in ts]

def run_procs(fn, k=4):
    ps = [mp.Process(target=fn) for _ in range(k)]
    [p.start() for p in ps]; [p.join() for p in ps]

if __name__ == "__main__":
    timeit("CPU x4 sequential", lambda: [burn() for _ in range(4)])
    timeit("CPU x4 threads (GIL)", lambda: run_threads(burn))
    timeit("CPU x4 processes", lambda: run_procs(burn))
    timeit("IO x4 sequential", lambda: [wait_io() for _ in range(4)])
    timeit("IO x4 threads", lambda: run_threads(wait_io))
```

Expect threads to give no speedup for the CPU case (and sometimes a slowdown), processes to scale with the number of cores you have (on a single-core machine they will not help), and threads to make the I/O case about four times faster. In a test run on a one-core sandbox with Python 3.12, the CPU cases all took about 0.6 seconds, while the I/O case dropped from 2.0 to 0.5 seconds with threads. In recent Python versions there is an optional free-threaded build without the GIL; treat results as version-dependent.

**2) A race condition, then the fix:**

```python
import threading

counter = 0
lock = threading.Lock()

def unsafe(n):
    global counter
    for _ in range(n):
        counter += 1                      # read, add, write: not atomic

def safe(n):
    global counter
    for _ in range(n):
        with lock:
            counter += 1

def run(worker, n=200_000, k=4):
    global counter
    counter = 0
    ts = [threading.Thread(target=worker, args=(n,)) for _ in range(k)]
    [t.start() for t in ts]; [t.join() for t in ts]
    return counter

print("expected", 4 * 200_000)
print("unsafe  ", run(unsafe))            # may be lower: lost updates (version-dependent)
print("safe    ", run(safe))              # always exact
```

How often the unsafe version loses updates depends on the Python version and timing, but the bug is real in any language: a correct program must not rely on luck.

**3) A tiny event-loop echo server with `epoll`-backed selectors**, one thread serving many clients:

```python
import selectors, socket

sel = selectors.DefaultSelector()          # epoll on Linux, kqueue on macOS

def accept(server):
    conn, _ = server.accept()
    conn.setblocking(False)
    sel.register(conn, selectors.EVENT_READ, handle)

def handle(conn):
    data = conn.recv(4096)                 # will not block: the selector said it is ready
    if data:
        conn.sendall(data)                 # fine for a demo; real servers handle partial writes
    else:
        sel.unregister(conn); conn.close()

server = socket.socket()
server.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_REUSEADDR, 1)
server.bind(("127.0.0.1", 9000)); server.listen(); server.setblocking(False)
sel.register(server, selectors.EVENT_READ, accept)

while True:
    for key, _ in sel.select():            # sleeps in the kernel until something is ready
        key.data(key.fileobj)              # call accept() or handle()
```

Run it, then connect several terminals with `nc 127.0.0.1 9000`; while it waits, run `strace -p $(pgrep -f echo_server) -e trace=epoll_wait` (on Linux) to see the loop sleeping in `epoll_wait`. Add `time.sleep(5)` inside `handle` and watch every other client freeze: a blocking call in the loop stalls everyone.

**4) Look at your own process through the kernel's eyes** (Linux):

```python
import os, mmap, resource

def status(keys=("Name", "VmRSS", "VmSize", "Threads")):
    with open(f"/proc/{os.getpid()}/status") as f:
        for line in f:
            if line.split(":")[0] in keys:
                print(line.strip())

def faults():
    return resource.getrusage(resource.RUSAGE_SELF).ru_minflt

status()
before = faults()
blob = mmap.mmap(-1, 200 * 1024 * 1024)     # anonymous mapping: address space now, RAM later
status()                                    # VmSize jumps; VmRSS barely moves (lazy allocation)
print("faults after mapping:", faults() - before)
for i in range(0, len(blob), 4096):
    blob[i] = 1                             # first touch of each 4 KB page triggers a minor page fault
status()                                    # now VmRSS reflects the touched memory
print("faults after touching:", faults() - before)
print("fd limit:", resource.getrlimit(resource.RLIMIT_NOFILE))
```

In a test run, virtual size jumped by about 200 MB immediately while resident memory stayed flat at roughly 9 MB, and touching the pages produced about 51,200 minor page faults (200 MB divided by 4 KB pages) and raised resident memory to match. That is lazy allocation made visible. (Plain `bytearray(n)` would not show this, because Python zero-fills it and so touches every page up front.) On macOS there is no `/proc`; use `ps -o rss,vsz -p PID`.

## In real products

- **Nginx, Redis, Node.js and HAProxy** are single-threaded or few-threaded event loops built on `epoll` or `kqueue`, which is how they serve very large numbers of connections cheaply.
- **Databases** (Postgres, MySQL, Kafka) depend on the page cache, `fsync`, memory-mapped files and carefully chosen process or thread models; tuning them (shared buffers, `vm.swappiness`, dirty page ratios, huge pages) is operating-system tuning.
- **Docker and Kubernetes** are applications of namespaces and cgroups; CPU throttling and OOM kills at "limits" are cgroup behavior, and a pod's `137` exit code is the OOM killer.
- **Browsers** use one process per site or tab for isolation (a crash or exploit stays contained), trading memory for security; **Chrome's** site isolation is a well-known example.
- **Python and Node services** scale CPU-bound work with multiple worker processes (Gunicorn, uvicorn workers, Node cluster or worker threads) because of the GIL and the single-threaded event loop, and scale I/O-bound work with async code.
- **Cloud providers** run customer VMs on hypervisors (KVM, Xen-derived, Hyper-V) and lightweight microVMs (Firecracker, used by AWS Lambda and Fargate) to combine VM-level isolation with container-like startup speed.

> [!pitfall] Adding more threads or workers to fix slowness. If the work is CPU-bound in Python, threads do nothing; if it is memory-bound, more workers multiply memory use and trigger the OOM killer; if it is I/O-bound on one slow dependency, more concurrency can overload it. Measure what the bottleneck is (CPU, memory, I/O, a lock, a downstream service) before scaling.
> [!pitfall] Blocking the event loop. A synchronous file read, a large JSON parse or a CPU-heavy loop inside a Node handler or an asyncio coroutine delays every other request. Move such work to a thread or process pool, a worker, or a queue.
> [!pitfall] Trusting "free memory" or VSZ. Linux uses spare RAM as page cache, so low `free` is normal; look at `available`, RSS, and whether the system is swapping. A huge virtual size is usually harmless.
> [!pitfall] Assuming a successful write is durable. `write()` returning means the kernel has the data, not the disk. If losing the last seconds on power failure is unacceptable, you need `fsync` (or a database that does it correctly) and hardware that honors it.
> [!pitfall] Ignoring signals and PID 1 in containers. If your app is PID 1 and does not handle SIGTERM, `docker stop` waits ten seconds and then SIGKILLs it, dropping in-flight requests; zombies pile up if nobody reaps children. Handle SIGTERM for graceful shutdown, and use a minimal init (`tini`, `docker run --init`) when you spawn subprocesses.
> [!security] Isolation is the OS's job, and it is only as strong as its configuration. Run services as unprivileged users, drop capabilities, use read-only filesystems and seccomp profiles where you can, remember that containers share the host kernel (so patch it), and never mount the Docker socket into a container you do not fully trust.
> [!prod] Watch the signals the OS gives you: load average against core count, CPU steal and iowait, memory `available`, swap activity, OOM-kill events (`dmesg` and container restart reasons), open file descriptors against the limit, and context-switch rate. Set explicit memory and CPU limits and alert before they bite.
> [!cost] Right-sizing is OS knowledge applied to money: most services are memory-bound or I/O-bound, not CPU-bound, so check which resource is actually saturated before buying bigger instances. Fewer, well-tuned processes often beat many idle ones, and an event-driven design can serve the same traffic on a fraction of the hardware.
> [!tip] When a program behaves strangely, ask the kernel: `strace` (what syscalls and where is it blocked), `lsof` (what files and sockets are open), `/proc/PID/status` and `/proc/PID/limits`, `dmesg` (OOM kills and hardware errors), `vmstat 1` and `iostat -x 1` (system-wide pressure). Ten minutes with these usually beats an hour of guessing.
q: Why does adding threads not speed up CPU-bound Python code, and what does?

The GIL lets only one thread execute Python bytecode at a time, so CPU-bound threads take turns. Use multiple processes (or native extensions that release the GIL) to use several cores; threads still help I/O-bound work.
What is a page fault and why can the cost vary so much?

A page fault happens when a page is not yet mapped. A minor fault maps or allocates a page already in memory (about a microsecond); a major fault reads from disk or swap (milliseconds), thousands of times slower.
What does exit code 137 usually mean in a container?
128 plus 9: the process was killed with SIGKILL, most often by the kernel's OOM killer because the container hit its memory limit. Investigate leaks, unbounded caches, limits and worker counts.
How can one thread serve thousands of connections, and what is the catch?
It uses non-blocking I/O with epoll or kqueue: wait for readiness, handle ready sockets, repeat. The catch is that any blocking or CPU-heavy call in the loop stalls every connection.
Why is a successful write() not proof the data is on disk?

write() normally copies data into the kernel's page cache and returns. The kernel flushes later, so a power loss can lose it. fsync forces data to stable storage, which is why databases call it on commit.
What are the four conditions for deadlock and how do you prevent it?
Mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption and circular wait. Break one: acquire locks in a single global order, use timeouts or try-locks, or hold fewer locks.
